outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of *Santos v. Kimmel*, detailing the specific interactions between former Congressman Santos and Jimmy Kimmel via the Cameo platform. It outlines the procedural history, explaining how the case reached the Second Circuit on appeal from a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, and defines the scope of appellate review regarding factual allegations and judicial notice.
subtopics: The 'Will Santos Say It?' segments: Creation of videos by Santos and subsequent airing by Kimmel/ABC
The deception strategy: Kimmel's use of fictitious identities to solicit videos
District Court proceedings: Dismissal based on fair use and preemption/failure to state a claim
Standard of Review: De novo review of 12(b)(6) dismissal and the role of judicial notice

outline.chapter_title: Copyright Infringement and the Transformative Nature of Parody
outline.description: This section provides a deep dive into the court's analysis of the four statutory fair use factors under 17 U.S.C. § 107. It focuses heavily on the 'purpose and character' prong, specifically analyzing why Kimmel's use was deemed transformative despite Santos's involvement in creating the original work. The chapter also addresses Santos's argument regarding 'bad faith' due to deceptive solicitation.
subtopics: Overview of the four fair use factors under Section 107
'Purpose and Character': Determining transformativeness through a reasonable observer lens rather than subjective intent
Addressing the 'Bad Faith' argument: Why deceptive solicitation does not negate fair use in commentary contexts
'Nature,' 'Amount,' and 'Market Effect': Analysis of published works and lack of market substitution

outline.chapter_title: Preemption vs. Independent Failure to State a Claim for Contract Actions
outline.description: Here, the text examines the disposition of Santos's state law claims for breach of contract (direct) and breach of implied contract. While acknowledging the preemption debate, this chapter explains why the court bypassed that complex issue entirely by ruling that Santos failed to meet basic pleading requirements under both Illinois law (third-party beneficiary status) and New York law (essential terms and meeting of minds).
subtopics: The Preemption Question: Why the court declined to resolve whether Copyright Act preempts these specific claims
Direct Breach Claim Analysis: Third-party beneficiary status under Illinois law applied to Cameo Terms of Service
Implied-in-Fact Contract Analysis: The requirement for specific terms and a mutual meeting of minds under New York law
Pleading Deficiencies: How conclusory allegations failed to satisfy Rule 8(a)

outline.description: A focused examination of why Santos's fraudulent inducement claim failed independently. This chapter clarifies the specific element required under New York tort law—the necessity of alleging actual out-of-pocket loss—and explains how Santos's complaint fell short by failing to connect Kimmel's deception to any quantifiable financial injury distinct from general reputational harm or lost licensing opportunities.
subtopics: Elements of Fraudulent Inducement under New York Law (*Lama Holding*)
'Out-of-Pocket Loss': Distinguishing compensable damages from speculative or intangible harms
[Application]: Why no actual pecuniary loss was alleged in relation to Kimmel's false representations
